title: Overview
body: Python · Rust · macOS / Windows / Linux Audio for Python, without ffmpeg. sound_rs plays and decodes the formats people actually have — MP3, FLAC, WAV, OGG, M4A — from a single wheel. The decoders are compiled in; no ffmpeg binary is required. Linux needs the ALSA runtime, and array APIs need NumPy. First sound 11 ms on a 10-minute file Memory 43 MB while streaming that file Import 1.1 ms versus 32 ms for soundfile Platforms 3 Linux, Windows, macOS Timing and memory figures above are historical 0.3.0 measurements on one Mac, not device guarantees. See the benchmark methodology and limits . pip install sound_rs import sound_rs with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("music.flac") # streams from disk, returns immediately player.seek(42.0) print(player.position, player.duration) player.wait() What it does Playback of files and NumPy arrays, blocking or through a persistent player with pause, seek, volume and position. Streaming decode : file playback fills a bounded ring incrementally instead of retaining the whole decoded track. Decoding to arrays for analysis, one file at a time or in parallel. Recording from an input device to float32 arrays. Writing WAV in PCM16, PCM24 or float32; save a recorded take in one call. Metadata from the container header when complete, with decoding as a fallback. Typed : ships sound_rs.pyi and py.typed , so editors autocomplete every call. What it does not do No effects, mixing graph or plugin system. If you need a DAW-style graph, this is the wrong tool; if you need to play or load audio reliably, it is the right one. The benchmark page also says where it is slower than the alternatives. Where to go next Installation — platforms, wheels, Linux audio libraries. Quickstart — the five things most code does. Command line — soundrs --help without writing Python. The player — controls, seeking, lifecycle. Recording and writing WAV files . API reference — every function and method.
headings: What it does What it does not do Where to go next

title: Installation
body: 01 · Start Installation One command. Wheels carry the decoders, so no ffmpeg or development headers are needed. pip install sound_rs Requirements Python 3.10 or newer, CPython. Linux x86_64 or aarch64, Windows amd64, macOS arm64 or Intel — all ship wheels. NumPy for array playback, loading, writing and recording arrays: install with pip install 'sound_rs[numpy]' . Platform Wheel tag Python Linux x86_64 cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64 3.10+ Linux aarch64 cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_17_aarch64 3.10+ Windows amd64 cp310-abi3-win_amd64 3.10+ macOS arm64 cp310-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64 3.10+ macOS Intel cp310-abi3-macosx_10_12_x86_64 3.10+ The wheels use the stable ABI, so one file covers every Python from 3.10 up — the same wheel installs on 3.10 through 3.14. Anything else (musl, PyPy, other architectures) falls back to the source distribution, which needs a Rust toolchain. From source git clone https://github.com/Neksand/sound_rs cd sound_rs pip install maturin maturin develop --release Linux audio Playback uses ALSA through cpal . Most desktops already have the runtime library; a minimal container or server needs it explicitly: sudo apt install libasound2 # Debian / Ubuntu (libasound2t64 on 24.04+) sudo dnf install alsa-lib # Fedora The wheel links the ALSA runtime If the library is missing, import sound_rs fails at load time, not on the first play. Install the package above. There is currently no supported playback-disabled build feature; no external audio decoder is required. Check it works import sound_rs print(sound_rs.__version__) print(sound_rs.list_devices()) # [(0, 'MacBook Pro Speakers', True), ...] print(sound_rs.get_audio_info("song.mp3")) From a terminal, soundrs --help prints the same check as a command, with the documentation link. See Command line . No sound, or an empty device list? See Troubleshooting .

title: Quickstart
body: 02 · Start Quickstart Five recipes. Each one runs as written. Play a file import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("music.mp3") play_audio blocks until the track ends and releases the GIL while it does, so other Python threads keep running. It opens the output device for that one call. Play with controls import sound_rs with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("music.flac") # returns immediately player.volume = 0.6 player.seek(30.0) # jump to 0:30 player.pause() player.resume() player.wait() # block until it ends The player keeps the stream open, so starting the next track costs milliseconds instead of reopening the device. Details in The player . Play a NumPy array import numpy as np import sound_rs rate = 44100 t = np.arange(rate * 2) / rate mono = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * t)).astype(np.float32) sound_rs.play_array(mono, rate) # 1D, mono sound_rs.play_array(np.stack([mono, mono]), rate) # 2D, (channels, frames) 2D arrays are channels first The shape is (channels, frames) , not (frames, channels) . Passing (frames, 2) silently plays the wrong thing — check the shape. Inspect a file sample_rate, channels, duration = sound_rs.get_audio_info("music.m4a") print(sample_rate, channels, duration) # 44100 2 213.4 This reads the container header — about 1 ms regardless of file length. It decodes one packet only for AAC, whose container does not record the channel count. Decode to NumPy import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load("music.flac") # float32, (frames, channels) print(audio.shape, rate) This puts the whole file in RAM A 10-minute stereo FLAC becomes 211 MB. For playback use Player.play_file , which streams and stays under a few megabytes. Decode many files import sound_rs clips = sound_rs.load_many(["a.flac", "b.flac", "c.flac"]) # all cores, GIL released for audio, rate in clips: print(audio.shape, rate) Choose a device import sound_rs for index, name, is_default in sound_rs.list_devices(): print(("*" if is_default else " "), index, name) sound_rs.play_audio("music.mp3", device="MacBook Pro Speakers") Continue with The player .
headings: Play a file Play with controls Play a NumPy array Inspect a file Decode to NumPy Decode many files Choose a device

title: The player
body: 04 · Guides The player Player owns one output stream for its whole lifetime. Every method below acts on that stream, so starting a track never reopens the device. import sound_rs player = sound_rs.Player() # opens the default device player.play_file("first.flac") # returns immediately player.wait() player.play_file("second.mp3") # reuses the open device player.stop() del player # closes the stream Use it as a context manager with sound_rs.Player() as player: stops playback and joins the decoder on exit, including when an exception is raised. The output stream remains open until the player object is destroyed; a bound variable can keep it alive after the block. Lifecycle State What it means Leaves it idle Stream open, nothing loaded play_file , play_array playing Callback writes audio pause , stop , end of source paused Callback writes silence, position frozen resume , stop finished Source exhausted, stream still open Start another source; a retained file/array can resume, a finished feed must restart Controls Call Effect play_file(path) Streams a file from disk. Returns immediately. play_array(arr, rate) Plays an in-memory array; resampled to the device once, up front. pause() Stops producing sound and freezes position . resume() Continues an active source or replays a retained finished file/array. A stopped source or finished feed must restart. stop() Clears the source and queue, resets position, keeps the device stream open. seek(seconds) Jumps; works while paused. wait() Waits for completion/drain, or returns when paused/stopped (GIL released). del player Releases this reference; destroying the object stops the decoder and closes the stream. Seeking Seeking uses packet timestamps and drops decoded frames before the requested position. The source must be a file or an array, and the time finite; paused seeks preserve pause intent. Codec/container support determines positioning accuracy and seek cost. Seeking preserves pause and queued files. Non-finite positions raise SoundRsError(code="usage") ; a fed stream or stopped player cannot seek. After natural file completion, seek or resume restarts the current file, including the last file reached through a queue. player.play_file("track.flac") player.seek(90.5) # 1:30.5 player.wait() print(player.position) # ~ track length, not the seek offset Seeking past the end Requests beyond the track are clamped to the last frame. position keeps counting from the seek target, so duration and position stay in the same units. Volume Applied in the callback, so it changes instantly and does not touch the decoded data. Range is 0 to 4; values outside are clamped. Volume 1.0 is unity. player.volume = 0.25 # quiet player.volume = 1.0 # unity Position and duration Both are seconds, read from the audio clock, not from wall time. For files the duration comes from the container header and is available right after play_file . For arrays it is the array length divided by the sample rate. player.play_file("track.mp3") print(player.duration) # 213.4 print(player.position) # 0.0 print(player.is_playing) # True Queue enqueue requires an active file source started with play_file ; array/feed modes reject it. When the current file ends, the decoder opens the next and continues on the same stream. Rate and channel count may differ between tracks. Pausing preserves the queue. with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("first.flac") player.enqueue("second.mp3") player.enqueue("third.wav") print(player.queue) # ['second.mp3', 'third.wav'] player.wait() # plays all three Pushing audio from Python For synthesis or a network stream, feed samples instead of a file. feed blocks while the buffer is full, so a fast producer cannot exhaust memory. If the buffer cannot drain for five seconds — a paused player, for example — it raises SoundRsError with code="stalled" instead of hanging. The timeout measures consecutive time without ring progress, not the duration of a feed() call. Long healthy feeds are supported. Closing an empty feed completes cleanly; wait() includes the final output drain. end_feed() requires a fed source; after a finished feed, call begin_feed() to start another. import numpy as np import sound_rs player = sound_rs.Player() player.begin_feed(48000) for _ in range(100): block = (0.2 * np.sin(np.arange(4800) * 0.057)).astype(np.float32) player.feed(block) # returns when the buffer has room player.end_feed() player.wait() Feed at the device rate for clean joins Chunks are converted and resampled independently, so a non-device rate can click at chunk boundaries. Query player.sample_rate and feed that. Threading and the GIL File decoding runs on a Rust worker. Playback waits and feed backpressure release the GIL, so other Python threads can run. Array conversion/resampling, metadata queries, player shutdown joins and device setup/teardown can still hold it. Calling wait() on an event-loop thread still blocks that loop until playback completes. Create, use and destroy each Player or Recorder on the same thread. Even sequential use from a different thread is invalid. Separate threads may own separate instances; a worker may call sound_rs.play_audio because that function creates and disposes its own player there. Device selection import sound_rs print(sound_rs.list_devices()) player = sound_rs.Player(device="MacBook Pro Speakers") print(player.device, player.sample_rate, player.channels) The device is opened once, at construction. A backend failure is signaled atomically and reported as SoundRsError(code="device") ; create a new Player to reopen it. The two-second no-progress watchdog separately reports stalled . This is fault reporting, not automatic reconnection. The output callback never waits for its state mutex: contention produces silence for that callback, so hard real-time or zero-underrun behavior is not promised. Physical disconnect behavior still needs device testing on each platform.

title: Streaming and memory
body: 05 · Guides Streaming and memory play_file decodes incrementally. A decoder thread fills a one-second ring buffer, and the audio callback drains it. The ring size is independent of file length; container, decoder, resampler and process memory are additional. How it works When the sample rate changes, the resampler removes its filter delay and drains the filter tail at EOF. The output contains exactly ceil(input_frames * output_rate / input_rate) frames, including tracks shorter than a processing block. Seeking resets the filter and frame counters. This does not make independently resampled feed() blocks continuous; use the device rate for those blocks. The decoder thread reads a packet, decodes it to float32, converts the channel count and resamples to the device rate. The result goes into a ring buffer sized for one second of device audio. The audio callback pops samples from that buffer. When it is empty, the callback writes silence and keeps the stream alive. Seeking replaces the ring buffer and repositions the decoder; the old audio that was still queued is discarded and does not count towards the new position. Playback can start before the full file is decoded. Startup still depends on device setup, container probing and any resampler buffering. Numbers Historical 0.3.0 measurements: ten-minute stereo FLAC, 44.1 kHz, measured with bench/run.py on an Apple M5 Pro. These are not current hardware guarantees: sound_rs soundfile + sounddevice Time to first sound 11.3 ms 302 ms Peak RSS 43 MB 256 MB The competitor number is not a flaw in those libraries: their API takes an array, so the file has to be decoded before playback can start. Streaming is a different design. play_file or load? You want Use Memory Play a file Player.play_file ~1 s ring plus decoder/filter overhead Analyse the samples load whole file as float32 Play an array you already have play_array copied audio plus conversion temporaries Play a file, need the samples too load, then play_array whole file Ten minutes of 44.1 kHz stereo float32 is about 212 MB of sample payload. Decoding and resampling can need additional temporary buffers. import sound_rs # streaming: bounded playback ring, incremental decode with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("lecture-2h.m4a") player.wait() # analysis: everything in RAM, decoded in parallel with other files clips = sound_rs.load_many(["a.flac", "b.flac"]) Caveats duration for a streamed file comes from the header; a VBR MP3 without a frame count reports None until the decoder reaches the end. Seeking uses container indexes and trims decoded packets to the requested position. Accuracy and cost depend on the codec/container; an unindexed stream may require walking forward. load retains its decoded result (or requested window), and load_many retains every result in the batch.
headings: How it works Numbers play_file or load? Caveats

title: Formats and gapless
body: 06 · Guides Formats and gapless Built-in WAV, FLAC, MP3, Ogg/Vorbis and AAC-in-MP4 decoding, with encoder-delay trimming where metadata is available. Supported formats Format Extensions Decoder Notes WAV .wav symphonia PCM, including tested 24-bit and multichannel files FLAC .flac symphonia Lossless decode; supported codec layouts/rates MP3 .mp3 minimp3 / symphonia Full-file load uses minimp3; bytes/windows/streaming use Symphonia OGG Vorbis .ogg symphonia — AAC in MP4 .m4a, .mp4 symphonia priming read from the edit list There is no extension allowlist. Probing recognizes containers; a successful probe does not prove that every codec or packet inside is supported. Raw AAC and other containers need dedicated validation before relying on them. Gapless Lossy encoders add silence at both ends — a few thousand samples that are not part of the recording. Left in, every track gains a click of silence and offsets by a millisecond or two. sound_rs trims them: MP3 and OGG declare the delay and padding in the container. AAC in MP4 records the priming in an edit list that symphonia parses but does not expose, so the library reads the elst box itself. Historical comparison: a 60-second AAC file decoded to 2 646 016 frames and agreed with ffmpeg to 8·10⁻⁸. AAC can retain less than one codec frame of tail padding; these measurements do not guarantee exact alignment for every file. import sound_rs, soundfile ours, _ = sound_rs.load("track.flac") theirs, _ = soundfile.read("track.flac", dtype="float32") print(ours.shape == theirs.shape, abs(ours - theirs).max()) # (True, 0.0) MP3 is offset by 47 samples The tested full-file MP3 path starts 47 samples (~1 ms) earlier than libsndfile and ffmpeg. The measured fixture lengths match and samples agree to 1.6·10⁻⁵ once aligned. Bytes, windowed and streamed MP3 use a different decoder; do not assume sample identity or alignment across these paths. Bit depth Everything is converted to float32 on decode. 24-bit files keep their resolution; there is no silent truncation to 16-bit anywhere in the path. On output the device decides the sample format — f32, f64, i16, i32, u8 or u16 — and conversion happens in the callback. When a file will not open Library failures raise sound_rs.SoundRsError , a RuntimeError subclass. Python argument conversion can instead raise TypeError or OverflowError . import sound_rs try: sound_rs.play_audio("broken.mp3") except sound_rs.SoundRsError as error: print(error) # Unsupported or corrupt audio file 'broken.mp3': ... Decoder errors normally fail the call. Unexpected end-of-file can return a decodable prefix, so a successful decode is not strict proof that the source file was complete. Checking without decoding import sound_rs sound_rs.is_supported_format("maybe.mp3") # True / False, header only sound_rs.get_audio_info("maybe.mp3") # (rate, channels, seconds) is_supported_format probes without decoding. get_audio_info uses complete header metadata when available, decodes a packet to discover missing format details, or decodes the file to determine an unknown duration. Its cost can grow with file length.

title: NumPy and arrays
body: 07 · Guides NumPy and arrays Two directions: arrays in for playback, arrays out for analysis. Both use float32 samples in the range −1.0 to 1.0. Shapes Call Shape Meaning play_array(mono, rate) (frames,) 1D, one channel play_array(stereo, rate) (2, frames) 2D, channel first load(path) (frames, channels) 2D, frames first The two directions have opposite layouts play_array takes (channels, frames) because that is how a matrix of channels is usually built; load returns (frames, channels) so audio[i] is one frame and audio[:, 0] is the left channel. Round-tripping needs a transpose: sound_rs.play_array(audio.T, rate) . Playing arrays import numpy as np import sound_rs rate = 48000 seconds = 3 t = np.arange(rate * seconds) / rate left = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 220 * t)).astype(np.float32) right = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 330 * t)).astype(np.float32) sound_rs.play_array(np.stack([left, right]), rate) The array is converted to the device layout once, before playback starts: channel folding, then one FFT resample if the rates differ. Playing a 48 kHz array on a 44.1 kHz device costs a few milliseconds and sounds correct — a naive nearest-neighbour resampler would alias. Decoding to arrays import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load("track.mp3") print(audio.shape, audio.dtype, rate) # (9437184, 2) float32 44100 print(audio[:, 0].max()) # peak of the left channel load returns the whole file. Ten minutes of stereo float32 is 211 MB, so for long files prefer streaming playback or decode one channel at a time from your own pipeline. Batch decoding import glob import sound_rs paths = sorted(glob.glob("dataset/*.flac")) clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths) # uses every core print(len(clips), clips[0][0].shape) Threads load_many(paths, threads=2) limits the pool. The default is one worker per core. Ordering matches the input list, and the first failing file raises. Pitfalls float64 arrays are rejected. NumPy's np.sin returns float64; cast with .astype(np.float32) or use dtype=np.float32 . Integer arrays are rejected. Convert to float32 and scale to −1…1 yourself; the library will not guess whether your int16 is scaled. Non-contiguous arrays are copied. A slice like audio[::2] still works, but you pay for the copy. play_array copies the data. The stream callback needs an owned buffer; that is one copy of the track, not two.

title: Coming from another library
body: 08 · Guides Coming from another library Most Python audio code is three lines. Here is what those three lines become. From sounddevice # before import sounddevice as sd import soundfile as sf data, rate = sf.read("track.flac") sd.play(data, rate) sd.wait() # after import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("track.flac") You lose the array, which you did not need for playback, and gain no ffmpeg and no per-call device setup. If you do need the samples, sound_rs.load returns them in the same shape as sf.read . For a persistent stream with pause and seek, sounddevice needs an OutputStream plus a callback queue; sound_rs.Player is that in one object. From soundfile # before import soundfile as sf data, rate = sf.read("track.m4a", dtype="float32") # after import sound_rs data, rate = sound_rs.load("track.m4a") AAC and M4A libsndfile cannot read MP4/AAC. That is the case where this swap is not optional. From pydub # before — needs an ffmpeg binary on PATH from pydub import AudioSegment from pydub.playback import play segment = AudioSegment.from_file("track.mp3") play(segment) # after import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("track.mp3") No subprocess, no temporary WAV, no ffmpeg install step for your users. The trade: pydub also does cutting, concatenation and format conversion, which sound_rs does not. From playsound / simpleaudio # before — one shot, no controls, format support varies by platform from playsound import playsound playsound("track.mp3") # after import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("track.mp3") The wheel includes the same decoder families on each supported platform. The playback wait releases the GIL; device setup and teardown still depend on the backend. What you gain, what you give up sound_rs soundfile + sounddevice pydub Formats WAV, FLAC, MP3, OGG, M4A WAV, FLAC, MP3; no AAC anything ffmpeg reads External tools none none ffmpeg binary Playback without loading yes no no Editing (cut, mix, convert) no no yes Platforms 3, wheels many any with ffmpeg
headings: From sounddevice From soundfile From pydub From playsound / simpleaudio What you gain, what you give up

title: API reference
body: 09 · Reference API reference Functions for files and arrays, plus persistent Player and Recorder classes. Library failures use sound_rs.SoundRsError ; Python argument conversion can raise TypeError or OverflowError . Module sound_rs.__version__ — the installed version as a string, for example "0.2.1" . class sound_rs.SoundRsError(RuntimeError) — library failures carry a stable .code ; see error codes . play_audio sound_rs.play_audio(file_path: str, device: str | None = None) -> None Plays a file and blocks until it ends, releasing the GIL while waiting for playback. Opens the output device for this call; startup cost depends on the backend and device. Use Player for repeated playback. file_path — a file with a supported container and codec. device — exact device name from list_devices() ; the default device when omitted. Raises SoundRsError for an unreadable file, a missing device, or a device that disconnects mid-playback. import sound_rs sound_rs.play_audio("music.flac") sound_rs.play_audio("music.flac", device="MacBook Pro Speakers") is_supported_format sound_rs.is_supported_format(file_path: str) -> bool Probes the container header. Does not decode or verify codec support and packet integrity. A missing or unrecognized file returns False . Probe time depends on the container and storage. get_audio_info sound_rs.get_audio_info(file_path: str) -> tuple[int, int, float] Returns (sample_rate, channels, duration_seconds) . Uses the header when complete; missing rate or channel information can require decoding a packet. If the header has no frame count, the file is decoded to measure duration. The returned duration is a number; this function does not return None . load sound_rs.load(file_path: str, sample_rate: int | None = None, mono: bool = False, offset: float = 0.0, duration: float | None = None) -> tuple[numpy.ndarray, int] Decodes to float32 with shape (frames, channels) , returning the array and rate. Optional sample_rate resamples, mono folds channels, and offset / duration select a window in seconds. Times must be finite and non-negative; a requested rate must be positive. Requires NumPy. Memory includes the returned audio plus decoder and conversion/resampling temporaries. Raises SoundRsError for an unreadable file or when the build has no NumPy support. offset and duration are finite, non-negative seconds. duration=0 returns an empty array. A requested sample_rate must be positive; invalid options raise SoundRsError(code="usage") before file access. mono=True averages channels before resampling. load_many sound_rs.load_many(paths: Sequence[str], threads: int | None = None, sample_rate: int | None = None, mono: bool = False) -> list[tuple[numpy.ndarray, int]] Decodes in parallel with a Rayon pool, releasing the GIL. Order matches paths . threads=None or threads=0 uses the automatic worker count. All files are processed, then the first failure in input order is raised. A requested sample rate must be positive, including for an empty batch. Optional rate and mono conversion apply to every file; the whole batch is retained in memory. clips = sound_rs.load_many(["a.flac", "b.flac"], threads=2) play_array sound_rs.play_array(array: numpy.ndarray, sample_rate: int) -> None Plays a float32 array: (frames,) for mono or (channels, frames) for multichannel. Converts to the device layout and resamples if the rate differs, then blocks until playback ends. Raises TypeError for an unsupported dtype/dimensionality, SoundRsError(code="usage") for invalid rates, channel counts or non-finite samples, and SoundRsError(code="device") for device failures. play_sine_wave sound_rs.play_sine_wave(frequency: float, duration: float, sample_rate: int) -> None Generates a mono sine tone at half scale and plays it. Useful for checking that audio output works at all. Frequency and duration must be finite and non-negative, and the sample rate positive; invalid values raise SoundRsError(code="usage") before a device opens. sound_rs.play_sine_wave(440.0, 1.0, 44100) cli sound_rs.cli() -> int Entry point for the soundrs console script; reads sys.argv and returns an exit code. You do not call it from Python — see Command line . write sound_rs.write(file_path: str, audio, sample_rate: int, subtype: str = "pcm16") -> None Writes float32 audio to a WAV file. The array is (frames,) for mono or (frames, channels) — the same layout load returns, so sound_rs.write(path, *sound_rs.load(src)) round-trips. Samples outside −1…1 are clipped. Subtypes: pcm16 , pcm24 , float32 . Samples must be finite and the rate positive. See Writing WAV files for memory and RIFF limits. Only .wav is accepted so far; any other extension raises SoundRsError with code="usage" . Returns nothing. The sample rate and channel count must be positive and fit the WAV header. NaN and infinity, incomplete frames, and files too large for classic RIFF are rejected with code="usage" before opening the destination. A file-write failure has code="io" . Encoding and disk I/O release the GIL after copying the array. Read-only and strided float32 arrays are accepted; float64 remains a TypeError . audio, rate = sound_rs.load("take.flac") sound_rs.write("take.wav", audio, rate, subtype="pcm24") load_bytes sound_rs.load_bytes(data: bytes) -> tuple[numpy.ndarray, int] Decodes bytes to a float32 (frames, channels) array and its sample rate. AAC-in-MP4 priming is read from the buffer's edit list. MP3 uses Symphonia here, while a full-file load uses minimp3; samples and alignment can differ. Malformed data can raise SoundRsError(code="format") ; an unexpected EOF may yield a decodable prefix. list_devices sound_rs.list_devices() -> list[tuple[int, str, bool]] Output devices as (index, name, is_default) . The index is only for display — pass the name to play_audio or Player . Recorder sound_rs.Recorder(device: str | None = None) Opens an input device. Raises SoundRsError with code="device" when there is no microphone or the OS denies access. Member Returns Notes start() None Starts capturing stop() (ndarray, rate) Stops and returns what was captured record(seconds) (ndarray, rate) start + wait + stop record_to(path, seconds, subtype="pcm16") None Capture in memory, then write a WAV device / sample_rate / channels str / int / int Device properties list_input_devices sound_rs.list_input_devices() -> list[tuple[int, str, bool]] Input devices as (index, name, is_default) . The name is what Recorder(device=...) accepts. Player sound_rs.Player(device: str | None = None) Opens one output stream and keeps it open. Device name matching is exact; the default device is used when omitted. Create, use and destroy it on the same thread. A with block stops playback on exit; the device stream closes when the object is destroyed. Methods Signature Returns Notes play_file(path) None Streams from disk, returns immediately play_array(array, rate) None 1D or 2D float32 play_samples(samples, src_channels, sample_rate) None Interleaved Python sequence, converted to float32; no NumPy required pause() None Position freezes resume() None Continues an active source; a finished feed requires begin_feed again stop() None Clears source/queue and resets position; keeps device open seek(seconds) None Finite file/array target, clamped to known duration; preserves pause wait() None Waits for completion/drain or returns while paused/stopped; GIL released enqueue(path) None Requires active file source; up to 128 waiting entries clear_queue() None Drops everything queued begin_feed(rate) None Switches to samples pushed from Python feed(array) None Requires begin_feed; blocks on full ring, times out after five seconds without progress end_feed() None No more samples; finishes when the ring drains play_samples is an existing Python-exposed method. Supply complete interleaved frames: [left0, right0, left1, right1] with src_channels=2 . It copies the input and prepares it for the device, then returns while playback continues. Prefer play_array for NumPy arrays. Properties Name Type Notes device str Name the player opened sample_rate int Device rate channels int Device channel count volume float Read/write, clamped to 0…4 position float Seconds played duration float | None Seconds; None until known is_playing bool False when paused, stopped or finished queue list[str] Paths waiting behind the current track underruns int Ring-starvation callbacks after audio started; excludes silence from lock contention latency float | None Last device latency in milliseconds import sound_rs with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("track.flac") while player.position < 10: pass # do work while it plays player.seek(120.0) player.wait() Exceptions Raised by When SoundRsError Unreadable file, no output device, device disconnected, stalled stream, no NumPy support TypeError An array that is not a 1D/2D float32 ndarray OverflowError Python integer outside a Rust argument's representable range SoundRsError subclasses RuntimeError , so existing except RuntimeError handlers keep working.

title: Benchmarks
body: 10 · Reference Benchmarks Historical 0.3.0 measurements with the method next to them, including rows where the library is slower. These device measurements were not rerun during the current headless engineering validation and are not performance guarantees. Method Every measurement runs in a separate process : peak RSS is process-wide, so timing and memory cannot share one. Median and p95 over repeated runs; the corpus is generated by the harness so it is reproducible. Correctness is checked in the same run: decoded PCM is compared with libsndfile. Hardware: Apple M5 Pro, macOS 26.6.2, Python 3.14.7, release build with lto = "fat" and opt-level = 3 . Scoreboard Axis sound_rs Competitor Ratio Import, cold process 1.1 ms 31.8 ms (soundfile) 29× Metadata, 60 s file 1.2 ms 31.7 ms 26× Decode WAV 130 ms 157 ms 1.2× Decode FLAC 265 ms 455 ms 1.7× Decode MP3 241 ms 268 ms 1.1× Decode AAC 349 ms not supported — Time to first sound, 10 min 11.3 ms 302 ms 27× Peak RSS, 10 min file 43 MB 256 MB 6× Playback overhead, 3 s tone 30 ms 241 ms 8× Batch decode, 2 FLAC files 177 ms 299 ms 1.7× Decode detail 60 seconds of stereo 44.1 kHz, median and p95 over seven runs. Format sound_rs libsndfile PCM check WAV 16-bit 131 / 160 ms 155 ms identical FLAC 265 / 267 ms 465 ms identical MP3 241 / 249 ms 268 ms 1.6·10⁻⁵, 47 samples offset M4A (AAC) 361 / 365 ms unsupported 8·10⁻⁸ vs ffmpeg Playback and memory First sound Peak RSS Overhead sound_rs Player, 10 min stream 11.3 ms 43 MB +30 ms soundfile + sounddevice 302 ms 256 MB +241 ms The playback overhead row is a 3-second tone: wall clock minus the track duration. The player number uses a stream that is already open; the one-shot play_array pays the device setup and lands around +180 ms. Reproduce it python bench/run.py # sound_rs only python bench/run.py --compare # + soundfile / sounddevice python bench/run.py --reps 9 The harness generates its corpus (3 s and 10 min, WAV plus MP3/FLAC/M4A when ffmpeg is available), runs each measurement in a subprocess, and prints median, p95 and peak RSS. A full run takes about three minutes on the machine above. Where it loses MP3 alignment : 47 samples (~1 ms) earlier than libsndfile and ffmpeg. Length is exact; values match after alignment. WAV decode : a memcpy race with libsndfile, 1.2× is all there is. AAC decode is slower than the other formats — a newer decoder with less tuning — though libsndfile cannot decode it at all. Very small files : for a 3-second tone the fixed device setup dominates everything, and all libraries land within a few tens of milliseconds of each other.

title: Troubleshooting
body: 11 · Reference Troubleshooting What to check when there is no sound, no device, or a call that blocks longer than expected. No sound sound_rs.list_devices() — if the list is empty, the OS sees no output device. sound_rs.play_sine_wave(440.0, 1.0, 44100) — if this is silent, the problem is the device, not the file. Check the system volume and the default output device; the player follows the OS default. On macOS, the terminal or IDE may need microphone/audio permission for output routing in some sandboxed setups. The device is busy SoundRsError: Cannot open output stream usually means another application holds the device in exclusive mode — a DAW, a call, or another Python process with an open player. Close one player before opening another, or use a different device: import sound_rs print(sound_rs.list_devices()) sound_rs.play_audio("track.mp3", device="Built-in Audio Analog Stereo") Linux: ALSA and PipeWire Playback goes through ALSA. On PipeWire systems install pipewire-alsa ; on PulseAudio systems install pulseaudio-alsa , so ALSA has a bridge to the sound server. In a container there is no sound server and no device: that is expected. Use load for decoding — it needs no audio device. Why the first play is slow play_audio and play_array open the output device on every call: roughly 0.1–0.2 s before the first sample. Player opens it once, which brings the overhead down to about 30 ms. with sound_rs.Player() as player: player.play_file("a.flac"); player.wait() player.play_file("b.flac"); player.wait() # no device setup The call blocks forever It should not. Playback without progress for two seconds raises SoundRsError: Playback stalled instead of hanging. If you see it, the device probably disappeared — reopen the player and retry. If you need playback in the background, use a thread or Player.play_file , which already returns immediately. Jupyter and notebooks Blocking calls work, but a long track freezes the cell. Use the player: player = sound_rs.Player() player.play_file("lecture.mp3") # the cell returns; more code runs while it plays player.position asyncio play_audio and wait release the GIL but they are still blocking calls. Off-load them: import asyncio import sound_rs await asyncio.to_thread(sound_rs.play_audio, "track.flac") MP3 samples do not line up with another library Different decoders trim the encoder delay slightly differently. sound_rs starts 47 samples (~1 ms) earlier than libsndfile and ffmpeg on LAME files; lengths match exactly. If you compare waveforms, align first. See Formats and gapless . "Input must be a 1D or 2D numpy array of float32" NumPy's maths returns float64 by default: samples = (0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * np.arange(48000) / 48000)) samples = samples.astype(np.float32) # required sound_rs.play_array(samples, 48000) Intel Macs and ARM Linux Only macOS arm64, Windows amd64 and Linux x86_64 have wheels. Elsewhere pip builds from source, which needs Rust. pip install sound_rs --no-binary sound_rs forces that path if a stale wheel is being picked up.

title: Changelog
body: 12 · Reference Changelog Unreleased — media validation Bounds-check MP4 box lengths before arithmetic and slicing. Cap metadata-driven initial decode reservations at 32 MiB; this is not a limit on total decoded audio memory. Validate WAV dimensions, sizes and finite samples before touching the destination; include odd PCM24 padding in RIFF size and classify write errors as io . Use checked NumPy read borrows; reject zero or overflowing channel counts. Reject invalid load/synthesis parameters and non-finite CLI volume. WAV encoding and disk I/O release the GIL. Unreleased — playback lifecycle Drain the final written audio prefix, complete empty feeds and time out only stalled producers. Paused wait returns without discarding the queue. Preserve pause/queue across seek, track the active queued file, and reject invalid source transitions, non-finite samples/volume, incomplete frames and zero rates. Report backend failures through an atomic flag and avoid blocking on callback state contention. Keep hardware recovery and continuous feed resampling as future work. Unreleased — bounded recording Move capture allocation and synchronization out of the input callback into a collector behind a bounded ring; preserve the 230 M sample storage limit. Report overflow, allocation and device faults; drain final input on shutdown and release the GIL while joining the collector. Make the documented record_to(..., subtype="pcm16") default effective at runtime and include context manager methods in the type stub. Unreleased — streaming resampler Drain filter delay at EOF even when input ends on a full block, remove startup delay for very short tracks, and trim output padding to the exact converted frame count. Test numerical output against a full filter pass across packet sizes, sample rates, stereo channels and impulses at the end of a track. Full-decode fixtures are unchanged. Short history. Full notes with diffs live on GitHub Releases . 0.4.0 recording era — writing files sound_rs.write(path, audio, rate, subtype=) writes WAV in PCM16, PCM24 or float32. Arrays are (frames, channels) , matching load , so a load/write round-trip needs no transpose. Recorder.record_to(path, seconds, subtype=) records and saves in one call. Non-contiguous arrays ( audio[:, 0] ) are accepted by write and play_array instead of raising. 0.3.2 accuracy load_bytes trims AAC priming too: the MP4 edit list is read from the buffer, so bytes decode to the same frame count as a file. record(seconds) never returns more than the requested frames; the extra device buffer at the end is cut. 0.3.1 documentation PyPI carries the corrected README: roadmap, and one figure for time-to-first-sound. 0.3.0 reliability, datasets, recording Stable error codes, mutation fuzzing, deterministic decode hashes, underrun and latency reporting. load(..., sample_rate, mono, offset, duration) , load_bytes , Recorder , Player.enqueue , begin_feed/feed . Benchmark harness v2 and abi3 wheels for five platforms. 0.2.2 command line soundrs console command: play , info , devices , docs , --version , --help . Documentation link in the package metadata. 0.2.1 packaging and metadata sound_rs.__version__ . Metadata for discovery: keywords, classifiers, documentation links; wheels and requires-python now agree on Python 3.10+. Small internal cleanups; no behaviour change. 0.2.0 streaming player Player with play, pause, resume, stop, seek, volume, position, duration. Streaming decode: constant memory, ~11 ms to first sound on a 10-minute file. rubato resampler replaces linear interpolation; downsampling no longer aliases. MP3 decoded with minimp3 (1.1× faster than libsndfile, previously slower). load_many , list_devices , device selection, typed stubs, SoundRsError . 0.1.8 correctness Gapless trimming for MP3 and OGG; AAC priming read from the MP4 edit list. Metadata without decoding; header-only duration. Playback waits for the exact device drain time instead of a fixed 100 ms. 0.1.7 builds Wheels for Linux, Windows and macOS across Python 3.10–3.14, published from CI.

title: Command line
body: 03 · Start Command line Installing the package also installs soundrs . It exists so that a minute after pip install you can check that audio works and find the docs, without writing Python. soundrs --help sound_rs — audio for Python Usage soundrs <command> [options] soundrs play <file> [--device <name>] [--volume <0-4>] soundrs info <file> soundrs devices soundrs docs soundrs --version soundrs --help Commands play Play a file and wait until it ends. --device <name> output device, see `soundrs devices` --volume <number> 0 to 4, default 1 info Sample rate, channels and duration, read from the header only. devices Output devices, one per line. docs Print the documentation link. Links Documentation https://neksand.github.io/sound_rs/ Source https://github.com/Neksand/sound_rs Commands Command What it does soundrs play FILE Plays a file and waits. --device picks an output device, --volume takes 0…4. soundrs info FILE Sample rate, channel count and duration from the container header — no decoding. soundrs devices Output devices, the default marked with * . soundrs docs Prints the documentation URL, for scripts and open $(soundrs docs) . soundrs --version Version on one line, safe to parse. sound-rs is installed as an alias of the same command. Examples # does audio work at all? soundrs play ~/Music/test.flac # which device names can I pass to Player(device=...)? soundrs devices # what is this file before writing any code? soundrs info podcast.m4a $ soundrs info podcast.m4a file podcast.m4a sample rate 44100 Hz channels 2 duration 42:13.6 (2533.612 s) Exit codes 0 success, 1 runtime failure (unreadable file, no device), 2 bad usage. Errors go to stderr, so the commands compose in shell pipelines. Checking an install After pip install sound_rs : soundrs --version # soundrs 0.2.2 soundrs devices # a device list means the audio backend loaded soundrs play test.wav # actual output If any of these fail with an import or library error, the audio backend did not load — see Troubleshooting . Decoding and soundrs info do not need an output device at all.

title: Datasets and ML
body: 08 · Guides Datasets and ML Most dataset code wants the same thing: 16 kHz, mono, one array per file, as fast as the machine allows. That is one call. One call import glob import sound_rs paths = sorted(glob.glob("dataset/**/*.flac", recursive=True)) clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths, sample_rate=16000, mono=True) for audio, rate in clips[:3]: print(audio.shape, rate) # (frames, 1), 16000 load_many decodes in parallel with the GIL released. On two FLAC files the harness measures 168 ms against 301 ms for a soundfile loop; the gap grows with file count until the cores are saturated. One file, converted import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load( "clip.m4a", sample_rate=16000, # resampled with an anti-aliasing filter mono=True, # channels averaged ) assert audio.dtype == "float32" and audio.ndim == 2 The order is fixed: fold channels first, then resample. Resampling before folding would do the same work twice on stereo. A window, not the whole file # first 10 seconds at 16 kHz, without decoding the rest audio, rate = sound_rs.load("lecture.m4a", duration=10.0, sample_rate=16000) # 30 s starting at 5 minutes audio, rate = sound_rs.load("lecture.m4a", offset=300.0, duration=30.0) Windows come from the streaming reader offset uses packet timestamps and trims leading decoded frames. A bounded duration stops decoding after the requested window; seek accuracy and the work needed to reach it depend on the codec/container. Memory Task Sample payload / observation Decode 10 min 44.1 kHz stereo to float32 About 212 MB of audio Return 10 min as 16 kHz mono 38.4 MB of returned samples Stream the same file for playback Bounded one-second ring plus overhead; historical 43 MB RSS Returned sample size is not peak RAM: decoding, channel conversion and resampling can temporarily retain larger source and destination buffers together. Resampling to 16 kHz mono is not just faster downstream — it is 5× less memory than keeping 44.1 kHz stereo. Choosing the thread count clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths, threads=4) # explicit clips = sound_rs.load_many(paths) # one worker per core Decoding is CPU-bound, so the ceiling is the core count. Feeding more threads than cores does not help; the benchmark's scaling scenario measures 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers. When not to use this Training on the fly — decode once and store the arrays; repeated decoding of the same file is wasted CPU. Huge corpora — load_many returns everything at once. For a corpus larger than RAM, call load per file inside your own batching. Augmentation and feature extraction — not implemented. This library gets you clean float32 audio; the DSP belongs to your framework.

title: Recording
body: 09 · Guides Recording The mirror of playback: one input stream, float32 samples, and the same error contract. import sound_rs print(sound_rs.list_input_devices()) # [(0, 'MacBook Pro Microphone', True)] with sound_rs.Recorder() as recorder: audio, rate = recorder.record(5.0) # five seconds print(audio.shape, rate) # (240000, 1) 48000 Devices list_input_devices() returns (index, name, is_default) . Pass the name to the constructor: recorder = sound_rs.Recorder(device="MacBook Pro Microphone") print(recorder.device, recorder.sample_rate, recorder.channels) The rate and channel count are whatever the device reports; the library does not resample on input. Folding to mono does not change the rate: import sound_rs mono = audio.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) # still at the captured sample rate start and stop record(seconds) is the convenient form. For an open-ended take, use start() and stop() : recorder = sound_rs.Recorder() recorder.start() input("press enter to stop") audio, rate = recorder.stop() Writing a WAV Use the same frames-first float32 layout as load : import sound_rs with sound_rs.Recorder() as recorder: audio, rate = recorder.record(3.0) sound_rs.write("take.wav", audio, rate, subtype="pcm16") Microphone permission macOS and Windows ask for microphone access the first time. A denied permission raises SoundRsError with code == 'device' ; there is no silent fallback. Saving a take import sound_rs with sound_rs.Recorder() as recorder: recorder.record_to("take.wav", 5.0, subtype="pcm24") record_to captures the take in memory, then writes it; it is not incremental disk recording. For preprocessing or another destination, record to an array and use sound_rs.write , which writes the same (frames, channels) layout that load returns. import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.Recorder().record(5.0) sound_rs.write("take.wav", audio, rate, subtype="float32") Limits Create, use and destroy the recorder on its original thread. Capture starts when the device delivers its first buffer. Startup latency can make a timed take shorter than requested; the recorder does not add frames to hide it. The callback writes to a bounded input ring (normally one second, at most 4 MiB). A collector thread stores the take outside the audio callback. The recording limit remains 230 M float32 samples (920 MB of payload, roughly 40 minutes at 48 kHz stereo). This is not a cap on total process memory or a hard real-time guarantee. Input overflow invalidates the take with code="stalled" , the storage limit or allocation failure uses unsupported , and a backend failure uses device . The library does not return a successful partial take after these faults. stop() drains the final callback and joins the collector with the GIL released. record_to() records to memory before writing the WAV; it is not an incremental disk recorder. No resampling, mixing or effects on input — capture is raw device audio. Playback and recording use independent streams. Simultaneous access depends on backend and device support; there is no shared clock or synchronization guarantee.

title: Writing WAV files
body: 10 · Guides Writing WAV files write saves a float32 array as a WAV file. It accepts the (frames, channels) layout returned by load , or a one-dimensional mono array. It requires NumPy. import sound_rs audio, rate = sound_rs.load("source.flac") sound_rs.write("copy.wav", audio, rate, subtype="pcm24") Subtypes and sample values Subtype Encoding Bytes per sample pcm16 Signed 16-bit PCM (default) 2 pcm24 Signed 24-bit PCM 3 float32 32-bit IEEE float 4 All three accept finite float32 samples and clip values outside −1…1. Integer PCM quantizes the samples; no dither is added. Strided and read-only arrays are accepted through a checked copy. Float64 input is rejected rather than converted silently. Validation and errors The destination must have a .wav extension, the rate must be positive, and the channel count and byte rate must fit the WAV header. Invalid values or unsupported subtypes raise SoundRsError(code="usage") before opening the destination. File creation/write failures use code="io" ; Python dtype or integer conversion can raise TypeError or OverflowError . An existing destination is overwritten. Writes are not atomic: an I/O failure can leave an incomplete file. The format is classic RIFF WAV, not RF64; files beyond its size limits are rejected. Saving a recording import sound_rs with sound_rs.Recorder() as recorder: recorder.record_to("take.wav", 5.0, subtype="pcm16") record_to captures into memory and then calls the WAV writer. It does not stream samples to disk while recording. See capture limits . Memory and concurrency The writer copies the input and builds the complete encoded WAV buffer before writing it. Budget for the array, copied samples and encoded bytes together. Encoding and file I/O release the GIL after Python array preparation. Incremental writing and compressed output are not implemented.

title: Guarantees
body: 11 · Reference Guarantees A library is trustworthy when its promises are written down and tested. This is the list, and the ones that are deliberately not on it. Errors Library failures use sound_rs.SoundRsError (a RuntimeError ) with a stable .code . Python argument conversion can raise TypeError or OverflowError ; float64 arrays are rejected rather than silently converted. Code Meaning io The file could not be opened, read or written. format The container or codec was not understood, or no audio was decodable. device No output/input device, open failure or reported backend fault. stalled Playback/feed made no progress, or the recording collector could not keep up. unsupported The build lacks a feature (NumPy) or hit a documented limit. usage Invalid values, WAV dimensions or call order, for example feed() before begin_feed() . Codes are part of the API: renaming one is a breaking change. No panics on bad input The contract is to report malformed input without a panic crossing the Python boundary. Regression coverage in cargo test includes mutating every committed fixture ~200 times per file (bit flips, truncation, appended noise) and by feeding random bytes; every case must return Ok with finite samples or a non-empty error. This bounded test corpus is not exhaustive fuzzing or proof that arbitrary untrusted media is safe. Threads and the GIL Bulk decoding/writing, playback waits, feed backpressure and timed capture waits release the GIL. Python array preparation, player joins and device teardown can still hold it. Create, use and destroy each Player or Recorder on the same thread. Sequential cross-thread use is also invalid. Separate threads can own separate instances, subject to backend/device sharing limits. Determinism tests/decode_regression.py checks exact dimensions/rates for six fixtures, SHA-256 hashes of samples rounded to 10⁻⁴ for five, and an RMS tolerance for MP3. Missing fixtures fail the check. These are regression bounds, not a guarantee that every sample change is detected or that decoder output is bit-identical across CPUs and dependency versions. Memory Streaming playback uses a one-second ring; container, decoder, filter and process memory are additional. This bounds playback buffering, not total process RSS. load retains its result plus decoding/conversion temporaries; load_many retains the whole batch. The initial reservation ceiling is not a total decode-memory limit. Recording limits captured payload to 230 M samples (920 MB), with ring/process overhead additional. record_to and write also build an encoded WAV buffer. Historical streaming and soak RSS measurements are observations on one system; benchmark results are not memory guarantees. Audio quality Resampling uses rubato's FFT resampler: a 20 kHz tone downsampled to 24 kHz is filtered below 10% of its level instead of folding back as an alias. Encoder-delay/padding metadata is used when available; MP3 decoder paths differ and AAC can retain tail padding. See format limits . Historical test-corpus comparisons found identical WAV/FLAC PCM, MP3 agreement within 1.6·10⁻⁵ after a 47-sample alignment adjustment, and AAC agreement within 8·10⁻⁸. These are fixture results, not universal codec guarantees. What is not promised A latency figure. Latency depends on the OS, the device and its buffer; Player.latency reports what the backend measured, nothing more. Zero glitches or a complete glitch counter. Player.underruns counts ring starvation after playback starts. Callback lock contention produces silence without updating this counter; backend/device glitches are not fully observable. Real-time safety of the Python API. Calling feed() from Python is fine, but Python's scheduler is not a real-time scheduler. Bit-identical output across decoders. Different MP3 decoders trim delay differently; fixture comparisons do not establish equivalence for every file.
headings: Errors No panics on bad input Threads and the GIL Determinism Memory Audio quality What is not promised
